meaning: Number of darics given to the fund for rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 2:69)
description: The number 61000 appears in Ezra 2:69, where it indicates the amount of gold darics that the returning exiles gave to the building fund for the temple in Jerusalem. After the Babylonian exile, the Israelites returned under the leadership of Zerubbabel and began rebuilding the destroyed temple. The gifts – 61000 gold darics, 5000 silver minas, and 100 priestly garments – testify to the people's willingness to sacrifice and their devotion to God and his sanctuary. Although the number 61000 does not have an established symbolic value in biblical numerology, the context in which it appears is of great theological significance: the rebuilding of the temple represents the restoration of the covenant relationship between God and his people after the judgment of exile.

versions.meaning: The number 61,000 has no known specific symbolic meaning in biblical or Jewish tradition.
versions.description: The number 61,000 does not appear as a symbolically or theologically significant number in the Bible or in traditional Jewish numerology (gematria). It may occur in census contexts or similar settings in the Old Testament, but it is not assigned any deeper symbolic meaning. Symbolic significance in biblical tradition is usually linked to much smaller numbers such as 7, 12, 40, or 70.
versions.reason: [major] The description does not mention the specific biblical occurrence in Ezra 2:69, where 61000 darics of gold were given to the temple building fund. This is an important contextual reference that should be included.; [minor] The description too quickly dismisses symbolic relevance. Although 61000 does not have an established symbolic value, the context in Ezra 2:69 is theologically significant – it concerns the rebuilding of the temple after the exile, which is a central theme in Jewish theology.; [minor] The Meaning field should be updated to reflect the actual biblical occurrence in Ezra 2:69 as a contribution toward the rebuilding of the temple.

footnotes.text: A daric (Hebrew: אֲדַרְכֹּן, adarkon) was a Persian gold coin named after King Darius I. The use of this Persian monetary unit in the text confirms the historical context under Persian rule.

Some scholars debate whether the Hebrew אֲדַרְכֹּן (adarkon) in Ezra and דַּרְכְּמוֹן (darkemon) in Nehemiah refer to the same coin or different monetary units. Both are usually linked to the Persian daric.
The rebuilding of the temple after the exile is a central theme in prophetic and rabbinic literature. The Second Temple was completed around 516 BCE and stood until its destruction in 70 CE.
